---
# The Watch Left Running

The watch came to me in a cardboard box that smelled of cedar and cigarette smoke, along with a pawnshop receipt from Duluth dated 1971 and a sandwich bag of loose screws. There was no note. Just the watch: a silver Elgin with a cracked crystal and hands frozen at twenty past four.

I have repaired clocks for thirty-one years. Most of what people bring me is simple. A grandmother's mantel clock that needs oil. A wristwatch whose battery died during a divorce nobody talks about. You learn to read the story from the damage. A dropped watch has a different wound than a neglected one. This one had been opened many times. Some of the screws were scored by a flathead, others chewed up by something that slipped.

My father owned a pocket watch like this one. He wound it every night before bed, a ritual so constant I never thought of it as a choice. When he died, I found it in his nightstand, still running, because he had wound it that evening. I kept it for years without understanding why it mattered so much to me. Maybe it was the proof that someone had been keeping time for us, quietly, every day, without asking for credit. I think about that when a customer hands me something that has outlived its owner.

I opened the back. Pressed against the movement, where no one would see it unless they were looking, was a folded square of paper no bigger than a postage stamp.

It took me twenty minutes with tweezers to unfold it. The handwriting was small and slanted, the pencil gone silver with age.

*If you find this, the movement is sound. Wind it every morning. Don't let it stop.*

That was all. No name. No date.

I sat with that for a while. Then I did what I was trained to do, which was to think about the mechanism of the message. Who writes instructions to a stranger inside a watch? Someone who expected the watch to outlive them. Someone who was separated from the person meant to wear it. Someone who believed time was something you had to hold onto by hand.

I cleaned the movement over two evenings. The mainspring was tired but not broken. I set the jewels in an ultrasonic bath and watched the tiny gears turn under the magnifier as I reassembled them, each wheel meshing with the next like a sentence finding its grammar. I replaced the crystal with one I had in a drawer, left over from a job a customer never picked up. I oiled the pivots with a drop so small it was nearly a rumor. Working on old watches teaches patience the hard way. You cannot rush the escapement. You cannot force a bearing without cracking it. Every repair is a negotiation with a machine that was made by people who are now dead, and who built it to last longer than they did.

When I finally wound it, the second hand stuttered, hesitated, and then swept forward with a sound like a small heart finding its rhythm. I held it to my ear. I am not a sentimental man, but I stood in my workshop with the window open and the smell of rain coming in, and I listened to a stranger's watch keep time for the first time in decades.

I wondered who had been meant to wear it. Maybe a son who went to war and did not come home. Maybe a woman who left a town in the middle of the night and wanted her absence to have a tick to it, something that said *I am still counting*. Maybe a husband who wanted his wife to have a reason to wind something every morning, so that she would have to touch it, so that she would have to get up. Maybe nobody in particular. Maybe the writer was simply someone who believed small instructions matter, and that a thing properly cared for is a kind of promise.

People talk about objects as though they are dead things. But a watch is not dead while it runs. It does the one thing it was made for, every second, without rest and without applause. There is a dignity in that which I have come to respect more than most human ambitions. I have met men who spent their lives chasing fame and died forgotten. I have never met a clock that did not do its job.

I thought about writing a reply on the paper, or tucking in a note of my own for whoever came next. I considered it for most of an afternoon. In the end I did something smaller. I wrote the date on a fresh slip, and under it, in my clumsy hand: *Wound and running. Repaired by R. Haas.* Then I folded it and slid it back where the old note had been, so the watch would carry both voices, the one that had been waiting and the one that had answered.

I closed the back and placed the watch in a clean box with a tag for the owner. The owner, whoever they are, is due to pick it up Thursday, though I have no name and no number, only the receipt from Duluth. The tag says only *Returned*. It seemed the honest word. It also seemed to cover everything: the watch returned to service, the paper returned to its place, the old instructions finally followed.

Before I locked up, I checked it one more time. Twenty past four in the afternoon, and the hands were moving exactly as they should, carrying whatever they carry forward into the evening, ticking steadily toward whoever is waiting at the other end of the day.
---
